accept: layon then chaume premier cru then bonnezeaux and quarts de chaume with aubance and anjou coteaux de la loire outside

question.ans: Ascending: Coteaux du Layon, with its named villages such as Rablay, Beaulieu, Saint-Aubin and Saint-Lambert; then Coteaux du Layon Premier Cru Chaume, which demands successive hand-picked tries and a far higher residual sugar; then the two enclaves that stand alone — Bonnezeaux, on the three hills above Thouarcé, and Quarts de Chaume, promoted in 2011 to the Loire's only Grand Cru, with the region's highest must weight requirement at 298 g/L and its lowest yields. Outside the Layon valley altogether: Coteaux de l'Aubance, on the little Aubance river between the Layon and Angers, and Anjou-Coteaux de la Loire, on the Loire itself around and above Savennières. All are Chenin, all on Armorican schist, and all depend on autumn mist off small rivers — the same mechanism as the Ciron at Sauternes, at a smaller scale.
question.exp: The hierarchy is a ladder of required concentration and falling yield, and the two outliers are what catch candidates who memorised only the Layon. Coteaux de l'Aubance in particular is a value hunting-ground worth naming on a floor.

findings.claim: The model answer says the name Breton 'commemorates the Abbé Breton', Richelieu's steward in the seventeenth century.
findings.because: Rabelais already wrote of 'bon vin breton' from the Chinon country in Gargantua (1534), a century before the Abbé. So the name cannot come from him, and the Abbé story is a later legend. The answer's own mention of Rabelais contradicts its etymology.
findings.fix: Breton is the Loire's local name for Cabernet Franc. Tradition credits the Abbé Breton, Richelieu's steward, with spreading the vine through Chinon and Bourgueil in the seventeenth century, but Rabelais already praised 'vin breton' from Chinon in 1534, so the name is older than the Abbé.
findings.verifyReason: The finding holds. In Gargantua, chapter XIII (1534/35), Rabelais has Grandgousier promise "the good Breton wine, not that which grows in Britain, but in the good country of Verron". The Véron is the land where the Loire meets the Vienne beside Chinon. I confirmed this in the Project Gutenberg text of the Urquhart translation, line 3371. Dico-du-vin makes the same point against the Abbé Breton story. The Abbé was a seventeenth-century figure at Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil and is tied to Richelieu. English Wikipedia still repeats the story, and French Wikipedia lists "plant de l'abbé Breton" as a synonym, so the tradition is real. But the name was in use a century before him, so it cannot commemorate him. The model answer states the eponym as fact ("It commemorates the Abbé Breton") and then mentions Rabelais only as praising "the wine of Chinon". It never notices that Rabelais used the word "breton" itself, so a student learns a false etymology. The examiner's fix is right in substance. Two changes make it better: the fix should replace the whole model answer so the DNA and parentage part is kept, and it should say "the Véron near Chinon", which is what Rabelais wrote. No etymology is asserted in its place, because the true origin is not settled. The accept list's legend-based entries could stay as reported tradition, but the answer must not present the legend as fact.
verifySources: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/1200/pg1200.txt (Rabelais, Gargantua ch. XIII, Urquhart translation: 'the good Breton wine, not that which grows in Britain, but in the good country of Verron')
findings.finalFix: Breton is the Loire's local name for Cabernet Franc. Tradition credits the Abbé Breton, steward to Cardinal Richelieu, with propagating the vine through Chinon and Bourgueil in the seventeenth century and so giving it his name. But Rabelais had already written of 'the good Breton wine' of the Véron by Chinon in Gargantua (1534), a century earlier, so the name is older than the Abbé and the story is legend. The DNA matters more than the folklore: Cabernet Franc crossed with Sauvignon Blanc produced Cabernet Sauvignon, and crossed with Magdeleine Noire des Charentes produced Merlot; it is also a parent of Carmenère. In other words the Loire's grape is the ancestor of Bordeaux's, not a poor relation of them — the argument you make when someone calls Chinon a lesser claret.

question.ans: Breton is the Loire's local name for Cabernet Franc. It commemorates the Abbé Breton, steward to Cardinal Richelieu, who propagated the vine through Chinon and Bourgueil in the seventeenth century — though Rabelais had already praised the wine of Chinon a century before that. The DNA matters more than the folklore: Cabernet Franc crossed with Sauvignon Blanc produced Cabernet Sauvignon, and crossed with Magdeleine Noire des Charentes produced Merlot; it is also a parent of Carmenère. In other words the Loire's grape is the ancestor of Bordeaux's, not a poor relation of them — the argument you make when someone calls Chinon a lesser claret.
question.exp: Orals reward the answer that turns a nomenclature question into an argument. The parentage is also examinable on its own: know both crossings and the fact that Cabernet Franc's home ground is the Loire and the Basque country, not the Médoc.

findings.claim: The model answer says Vouvray and Montlouis are both 'one hundred per cent Chenin Blanc'.
findings.because: The Vouvray cahier des charges makes Chenin the principal variety and still allows Orbois (Menu Pineau) as an accessory variety. It is rarely used, but it is legal, so Vouvray is not 100% Chenin by law. Montlouis-sur-Loire is Chenin only.
findings.fix: Both are Chenin Blanc on tuffeau (Montlouis exclusively; Vouvray also permits a small accessory share of Orbois/Menu Pineau, now rarely used), and both run the full ladder from sec to moelleux plus pétillant and mousseux.
findings.verifyReason: The finding holds. The current INAO cahier des charges for Vouvray (the version that went to national opposition after the CNAOC opinion of 16 June 2020) says in Section V.1.a that the wines come from Chenin B as the principal variety and Orbois B as an accessory variety. Section V.2 caps Orbois B at 5% or less of the encépagement, counted per holding. So the model answer is wrong to call Vouvray "one hundred per cent Chenin Blanc" by law. Montlouis-sur-Loire allows Chenin B only. The examiner's fix is right. It avoids giving a percentage, which is sensible: French Wikipedia still says 10%, but the cahier I opened says 5% of plantings, not a share of the blend. If the owner wants a number, the fix can say "up to 5% of plantings". The rest of the answer and the accept list are not affected. I extracted the text from the INAO PDF locally after the web summary could not read it.
findings.finalFix: Both are Chenin Blanc on tuffeau (Montlouis exclusively; Vouvray also permits a small accessory share of Orbois/Menu Pineau, now rarely used), and both run the full ladder from sec to moelleux plus pétillant and mousseux.

question.ans: Both are one hundred per cent Chenin Blanc on tuffeau, and both run the full ladder from sec to moelleux plus pétillant and mousseux. Vouvray lies on the north bank of the Loire and is roughly five times the size, with deeper clay-with-flint perruches and limestone-rich aubuis over the tuffeau, colder sites, later ripening and the greater sweet-wine reputation — Huet and Foreau are its monuments. Montlouis occupies the plateau between the Loire and the Cher, on sandier, warmer, faster-draining soils that ripen earlier and lend themselves to dry wine and sparkling. It only separated from Vouvray in 1938, having been sold as Vouvray before, and took the name Montlouis-sur-Loire in 2002. It has since been by far the more daring appellation: Chidaine, Blot and their generation legislated pétillant originel, the ancestral method, into existence in 2007, and Montlouis is now the centre of the region's dry-Chenin avant-garde.
question.exp: The comparison rewards structure: same grape, same rock, different river position, different soil depth, different regulatory temperament. The last point is the interesting one — Montlouis outran its famous neighbour by writing new law rather than defending old.

findings.claim: The model answer says that to carry the AMW seal a wine must 'respect a yield cap'.
findings.because: AMW's early 'Integrity' criterion capped cropping levels (Spy Valley, 2021). In June 2024 AMW members adopted a minimum ripeness of 18 Brix at harvest for Sauvignon Blanc. The current AMW FAQ lists origin (100% Marlborough, inside the AMW-defined area), 18 Brix ripeness, bottling in New Zealand, sustainability certification and a blind sensory assessment. It sets no yield limit, and AMW says on the Wine Blast podcast that it dropped tonnage caps in favour of a ripeness rule.
findings.fix: Replace "respect a yield cap" with "meet a minimum ripeness of 18 Brix at harvest (the original yield caps were replaced by this ripeness rule in 2024), pass a blind sensory panel"
findings.verifyReason: I could not refute the finding. AMW's own current FAQ lists five criteria: 100% Marlborough fruit from inside AMW's defined area, a minimum of 18 Brix at harvest for Sauvignon Blanc, bottling in New Zealand, a sustainability certification (SWNZ, BioGro or equivalent), and a blind sensory assessment by a winemaker panel. None of them is a yield, cropping or tonnage limit, and the AMW home page does not mention one either. Spy Valley's post of 22 Sep 2021 shows that the original Integrity standard did cap cropping, at levels set by season and soil, and let a panel approve over-cropped wines. Harpers says members unanimously adopted the 18 Brix rule and a tighter area in 2024. So "respect a yield cap" is outdated. The model answer also leaves out the ripeness rule and the sensory panel, both of which are now core criteria. The examiner's fix goes further than the evidence I could open: Harpers does not say the yield caps were removed or replaced, and I could not check the podcast. The better fix therefore says only what the sources support: yield limits in the original standard, a ripeness minimum and no yield limit in the current one, which was revised in 2024. The rest of the answer holds (voluntary, industry-led, launched 2018, sustainability, bottled in NZ).
findings.finalFix: Replace "respect a yield cap" with "be made from grapes picked at a minimum ripeness (18 Brix for Sauvignon Blanc, a rule members adopted in 2024; the original 2018 standard set cropping limits instead, and the current criteria set no yield limit), pass a blind sensory assessment by a panel of winemakers"

question.q: What is Appellation Marlborough Wine, and what problem was it created to solve?
accept: a voluntary marlborough certification requiring 100 percent marlborough fruit bottled in new zealand
the amw seal created against bulk shipped marlborough sauvignon
appellation marlborough wine an industry mark launched in 2018
certification protecting marlborough from wine bottled offshore
question.ans: It is a voluntary industry certification, launched in 2018 by a group of Marlborough producers rather than by government. To carry the seal a wine must be made entirely from Marlborough fruit, come from sustainability-certified vineyards, respect a yield cap, and be bottled in New Zealand. The problem it addresses is bulk: enormous volumes of Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc had been shipped in flexitanks and bottled offshore under supermarket labels, sold cheap and often blended to a price, which was hollowing out the region's name at exactly the moment that name was its most valuable asset. The bottling clause is the sharp end of the scheme. It sits alongside, not instead of, the legal framework — Marlborough is a registered geographical indication under the Geographical Indications Act in force from 2017, registered in 2018, and the 85% labelling rules still apply nationally.
question.exp: The examiner is testing whether a candidate can distinguish a statutory geographical indication from a private quality mark, and whether they understand why a region with one dominant variety polices its own name. Compare it to the Gimblett Gravels trademark in Hawke's Bay, which likewise defends a boundary the law never drew. The through-line for New Zealand answers is that the 2008 glut taught the industry that volume without control destroys premium positioning.
